UNITED NATIONS (CNN) -- The United Nations humanitarian chief Wednesday criticized a two-day pause in the fighting between the Sri Lankan army and Tamil Tiger rebels as "inadequate." U.N. Nations humanitarian chief John Holmes said he would have liked a "proper humanitarian pause." John Holmes, the under secretary general for humanitarian affairs and emergency relief coordinator, told reporters that the 48-hour break in hostilities was not sufficient, even as fighting resumed in the northeast of the country. The brief cessation of hostilities was announced by the Sri Lankan government on April 12 and allowed the U.N. and its partners to bring in necessary aid, said Holmes. He said he would have liked a "proper humanitarian pause" that lasted longer than two days, but hoped the break allowed for some progress to occur. Secretary-General Ban ki-Moon had originally welcomed the announcement by the Sri Lankan government. However, Ban also expressed his concern that, "This is less than the full humanitarian pause of several days I had pressed for." But Ban added that the pause "is nevertheless a useful first step and an opportunity to move towards the peaceful and orderly end to the fighting now so badly needed." The government of Sri Lanka has been battling the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Elam (LTTE) rebels in a civil conflict that has lasted nearly 25 years. The LTTE has been declared a terrorist organization by 32 countries, including the United States and the nations of the European Union. As many as 70,000 people have been killed since the conflict officially began in 1983. The most pressing concern now, according to Holmes, is the fact that over 100,000 people are currently crowded in a "very small pocket of land" that is about five square miles, or about twice the size of New York's Central Park. "It is a very small area indeed for what we believe is very large number of people" Holmes explained. The crowded population, primarily comprised of Tamil civilians, is subject to the continuing Sri Lankan government assaults. The British and French foreign ministers released a joint statement as well on Wednesday, claiming that the LTTE is also using Tamil civilians as human shields. Holmes also called attention to the fact that the press has been barred from covering the civil strife in Sri Lanka. Ultimately, Holmes and the United Nations would like to see a peaceful end to the hostilities, but "its pretty clear, frankly, that a ceasefire as such is not something available at present circumstances."

UNITED NATIONS (CNN) -- The United Nations' humanitarian chief on Wednesday criticized the two-day pause in fighting between the Sri Lankan army and Tamil Tiger rebels as "inadequate."

John Holmes, the U.N. under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs and emergency relief coordinator, told reporters that the 48-hour break in hostilities had proven insufficient, particularly as fighting resumed in the northeast of the country. The brief cessation, announced by the Sri Lankan government on April 12, had allowed the U.N. and its partners to deliver essential aid, Holmes noted. He stated that he would have preferred a "proper humanitarian pause" of longer duration, though he expressed hope that the brief window had allowed for meaningful progress.

Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon had initially welcomed the Sri Lankan government's announcement, while also voicing reservations, stating: "This is less than the full humanitarian pause of several days I had pressed for." Nevertheless, he characterized the pause as "a useful first step and an opportunity to move towards the peaceful and orderly end to the fighting now so badly needed."

The Sri Lankan government has been engaged in conflict with the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) for nearly 25 years. The LTTE has been designated a terrorist organization by 32 countries, including the United States and the member states of the European Union. An estimated 70,000 people have died since the conflict formally began in 1983.

According to Holmes, the most urgent concern at present is that more than 100,000 people are currently confined within a "very small pocket of land"—an area of roughly five square miles, or about twice the size of New York's Central Park. "It is a very small area indeed for what we believe is a very large number of people," Holmes explained. This densely packed population, consisting primarily of Tamil civilians, remains exposed to ongoing assaults by Sri Lankan government forces.

In a joint statement issued Wednesday, the British and French foreign ministers alleged that the LTTE is likewise using Tamil civilians as human shields.

Holmes further drew attention to the fact that journalists have been barred from covering the conflict in Sri Lanka. While he and the United Nations remain committed to achieving a peaceful resolution to the hostilities, Holmes acknowledged, "It's pretty clear, frankly, that a ceasefire as such is not something available in present circumstances."

John Holmes, who serves as under secretary general for humanitarian affairs and emergency relief coordinator, stated to journalists that he had hoped for a more substantial "humanitarian pause" in the violence.

Holmes explained that this 48-hour ceasefire wasn't enough, particularly since combat had already restarted in the country's northeastern region. Sri Lanka's government had declared this temporary halt in fighting on April 12, which created a window for the U.N. and partner organizations to deliver essential relief supplies, according to Holmes. While he expressed a preference for a longer pause than the brief two-day window granted, he remained hopeful that some meaningful progress had been achieved during that time.

Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon had initially responded positively to Sri Lanka's announcement of the pause. Nevertheless, he voiced reservations, noting that "This is less than the full humanitarian pause of several days I had pressed for." He continued, however, by acknowledging that the pause represented "a useful first step and an opportunity to move towards the peaceful and orderly end to the fighting now so badly needed."

This conflict pits Sri Lanka's government against the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) in a civil war spanning almost a quarter-century. Thirty-two nations—including the United States and EU member states—have designated the LTTE a terrorist group. The death toll since fighting began in 1983 has reached an estimated 70,000 people.

Holmes identified the most urgent issue as the situation facing over 100,000 civilians packed into an extremely confined area—roughly five square miles, equivalent to about twice the size of Central Park in New York. "It is a very small area indeed for what we believe is very large number of people," he noted. This densely packed population, consisting mostly of Tamil civilians, continues to face ongoing military operations from Sri Lankan government forces.

In a joint statement issued Wednesday, the foreign ministers of Britain and France alleged that the LTTE has also been using these Tamil civilians as human shields.

Additionally, Holmes drew attention to the fact that journalists have been prevented from reporting on the conflict within Sri Lanka. While the U.N. and Holmes ultimately hope for a peaceful resolution to the violence, he acknowledged, "it's pretty clear, frankly, that a ceasefire as such is not something available at present circumstances."

# UN Officials Voice Concerns Over Brief Sri Lankan Ceasefire

United Nations humanitarian chief John Holmes has criticized the recently implemented ceasefire between the Sri Lankan army and Tamil Tiger rebels, describing the temporary truce as "inadequate" for addressing the escalating humanitarian crisis. Holmes stated he would have preferred a "proper humanitarian pause" that extended for a significantly longer duration, arguing that the brief window was insufficient given the scale of the emergency facing civilians trapped in the conflict zone.

The 48-hour ceasefire, announced by the Sri Lankan government on April 12, was designed to create a narrow window during which the United Nations and its humanitarian partners could deliver critical aid to affected populations before military operations resumed in the northeast region of the country. While the pause did allow for some relief efforts, officials have expressed frustration that the timeframe was too limited to adequately address the mounting needs of civilians caught in the crossfire.

Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon echoed similar reservations about the ceasefire's brevity, noting that it fell considerably short of the multi-day humanitarian break he had specifically requested from Sri Lankan authorities. Despite these concerns, Ban characterized the pause as "a useful first step," suggesting it could serve as a foundation for future negotiations aimed at ultimately ending the prolonged fighting between government forces and rebel groups.

This latest development occurs against the backdrop of a conflict that has persisted for nearly 25 years, pitting the Sri Lankan government against the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), an organization officially designated as a terrorist group by 32 countries worldwide. Since the conflict began in 1983, the violence has claimed as many as 70,000 lives, making it one of the longest-running and deadliest civil conflicts in South Asia.

Holmes identified the most pressing humanitarian concern as the dire situation facing more than 100,000 people—the majority of them Tamil civilians—who remain trapped in an extremely confined area. This population is currently crowded into a mere five-square-mile pocket of land, an area roughly twice the size of New York's Central Park, raising serious concerns about overcrowding, access to basic necessities, and the safety of civilians caught between advancing military forces and entrenched rebel positions.

# UN Official Slams Sri Lanka's Brief Ceasefire as Insufficient Amid Civilian Crisis

United Nations humanitarian chief John Holmes has sharply criticized Sri Lanka's recent 48-hour ceasefire between government forces and Tamil Tiger rebels, calling the brief pause in fighting "inadequate" to address the mounting humanitarian catastrophe unfolding in the country's northeast.

Holmes emphasized that the short truce fell far short of what was needed to provide meaningful relief to civilians caught in the crossfire. He called on both the Sri Lankan government and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) to agree to a significantly longer humanitarian pause—one that would allow aid organizations sufficient time to deliver critical supplies, evacuate the wounded, and help civilians escape the conflict zone safely.

"A 48-hour window is simply not enough time to address a crisis of this magnitude," Holmes stated, urging both sides to prioritize the welfare of trapped civilians over military objectives.

Despite these appeals, fighting resumed almost immediately after the ceasefire period concluded, dashing hopes for a sustained humanitarian corridor. The renewed hostilities have left more than 100,000 civilians trapped within an alarmingly small conflict zone—an area spanning just five square miles—with limited access to food, medical care, clean water, and safe shelter.

The situation represents one of the most dire humanitarian emergencies in the long-running Sri Lankan civil war, which has raged for nearly 25 years between government forces and Tamil separatist rebels seeking an independent homeland in the north and east of the island nation. The conflict has claimed an estimated 70,000 lives since it began, making it one of Asia's longest and deadliest insurgencies.

Aid organizations and international observers have expressed growing alarm over the plight of civilians trapped in the shrinking conflict zone, many of whom have been displaced multiple times as the fighting has intensified in recent months. With government forces pushing to eliminate the last remaining Tamil Tiger strongholds, concerns continue to mount over the safety and welfare of the tens of thousands of men, women, and children caught between the two warring parties, with limited options for escape and dwindling humanitarian access to the besieged area.

# The United Nations and CNN: Global News Coverage of International Diplomacy

The United Nations serves as the world's foremost intergovernmental organization, bringing together 193 member states to address global challenges ranging from peace and security to human rights and sustainable development. Founded in 1945 in the aftermath of World War II, the UN operates through various bodies including the General Assembly, Security Council, and numerous specialized agencies working across the globe.

CNN, as one of the world's leading news networks, has played a significant role in bringing United Nations proceedings and initiatives to a global audience since its founding in 1980. The network's extensive coverage of UN activities has helped shape public understanding of international diplomacy, humanitarian crises, and global governance issues.

## Media Coverage of International Bodies

News organizations like CNN provide critical coverage of UN Security Council meetings, General Assembly sessions, and major international summits. This coverage often includes:

- Live broadcasts of high-profile speeches by world leaders
- Analysis of Security Council resolutions and debates
- Coverage of humanitarian crises addressed by UN agencies
- Reports on peacekeeping missions around the world
- Documentation of climate negotiations and sustainable development initiatives

## The Role of Journalism in International Relations

The relationship between major news networks and international organizations like the UN highlights the importance of transparent journalism in democratic accountability. When CNN correspondents report from UN headquarters in New York or from field operations in conflict zones, they help bridge the gap between complex diplomatic processes and public understanding.

This coverage serves multiple purposes: informing citizens about global affairs, holding international institutions accountable, and providing context for complex geopolitical events that affect populations worldwide. The partnership between robust journalism and international institutions remains essential for maintaining an informed global citizenry capable of understanding and engaging with the challenges facing our interconnected world.

Through consistent coverage, networks like CNN help ensure that the UN's work—whether addressing conflicts, negotiating climate agreements, or coordinating humanitarian responses—reaches audiences far beyond diplomatic circles, fostering greater public awareness of international cooperation efforts.

# UN Humanitarian Chief Criticizes Sri Lanka's Brief Ceasefire as Insufficient

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka** — The United Nations' top humanitarian official sharply criticized Sri Lanka's government on Tuesday, calling a recently announced 48-hour ceasefire with Tamil Tiger rebels grossly inadequate to address the deepening humanitarian crisis facing tens of thousands of civilians trapped in the island nation's war zone.

The UN's emergency relief coordinator said the brief pause in fighting would do little to help civilians caught between government forces and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) in the country's northern conflict zone, where aid organizations have reported dire shortages of food, medicine, and clean water.

"A ceasefire of just 48 hours is simply not enough time to allow for the safe evacuation of civilians, the delivery of critical humanitarian aid, and proper medical treatment for the wounded," the official said in a statement released from UN headquarters. "We are calling on both parties to extend this window significantly and to guarantee safe passage for those trying to flee the violence."

Sri Lankan government forces have been engaged in a prolonged military offensive aimed at crushing the Tamil Tiger insurgency, which has waged a decades-long campaign for an independent homeland for the country's Tamil minority. The fighting has intensified in recent months, with government troops steadily reclaiming territory once held by the rebels.

Humanitarian organizations estimate that tens of thousands of civilians remain trapped in the shrinking conflict zone, facing dwindling supplies and limited access to medical care. Reports from within the area describe overcrowded makeshift shelters and hospitals overwhelmed by casualties from the fighting.

The Sri Lankan government defended the ceasefire as a goodwill gesture, with officials stating it would provide an opportunity for civilians to leave rebel-held areas. However, critics, including several international aid groups, argued that the short timeframe was unrealistic given the scale of displacement and the dangerous conditions civilians would need to navigate to reach safety.

The Tamil Tigers have not publicly committed to honoring the ceasefire, and previous truces during the conflict have been marred by accusations of violations from both sides.

The UN has repeatedly urged Sri Lanka to allow greater humanitarian access to the conflict zone and to establish a genuine safe corridor for civilians. International pressure has mounted on Colombo in recent weeks, with human rights organizations warning of potential violations of international humanitarian law by both government forces and the rebels.

The Sri Lankan government has largely resisted calls for a more comprehensive cessation of hostilities, maintaining that a prolonged ceasefire would allow rebel fighters to regroup and further endanger civilians by prolonging the conflict.

As the fighting continues, the UN and other international bodies are expected to keep pressing both sides for expanded humanitarian access, though a resolution to the broader conflict remains elusive.

*This is a developing story.*

# UN Officials Voice Concern Over Sri Lanka Ceasefire as Civilian Toll Mounts

**GENEVA/NEW YORK** — Senior United Nations officials have expressed cautious concern over the situation in Sri Lanka following reports of a pause in fighting between government forces and Tamil Tiger rebels, with humanitarian coordinators warning that civilians remain trapped in dangerous conditions despite any lull in hostilities.

John Holmes, the UN's then-Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator, addressed the situation during briefings on the conflict, emphasizing that any pause in fighting must translate into genuine humanitarian access and protection for civilians caught in the crossfire in the island nation's northern conflict zone.

Holmes reportedly stressed that tens of thousands of civilians remained trapped in a shrinking strip of territory controlled by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), with limited access to food, medical care, and clean water. He called for both the Sri Lankan government and rebel forces to ensure safe passage for civilians seeking to flee the combat zone, and urged unimpeded humanitarian access to assess and address the deteriorating conditions on the ground.

## Ban Ki-moon's Response

UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon also weighed in on the escalating crisis, expressing deep concern over mounting civilian casualties and the humanitarian toll of the prolonged conflict. Ban called on both parties to the conflict to observe international humanitarian law and to protect civilian lives, urging an end to the fighting to allow for the evacuation of trapped non-combatants.

The Secretary-General's office reiterated appeals for a genuine cessation of hostilities—not merely a temporary pause—to allow humanitarian organizations to deliver aid and evacuate the sick, wounded, and vulnerable populations, including children and the elderly, from the conflict zone.

## Civilian Casualties Under Scrutiny

The comments came amid growing international alarm over reports of high civilian casualties in the conflict zone, with rights groups and UN officials citing credible accounts of shelling in areas where civilians had sought shelter, including in designated "safe zones." Estimates of the death toll varied, but UN officials acknowledged that verified figures were difficult to obtain given restricted access for independent monitors and journalists to the combat areas.

Both the Sri Lankan government and the LTTE faced criticism from UN officials over allegations of endangering civilian lives — the government over shelling in proximity to civilian concentrations, and the LTTE over allegations of using civilians as human shields and preventing them from leaving the conflict zone.

## Calls for Accountability

UN officials, including Holmes, called for independent investigations into alleged violations of international humanitarian law by all parties to the conflict. The UN also pressed for humanitarian corridors to be established and respected, allowing aid convoys to reach displaced populations and enabling civilians to leave areas of active combat.

The international community continued to monitor the situation closely, with the UN Security Council and humanitarian agencies pressing for greater transparency and access as the conflict in Sri Lanka's north approached its final, and most devastating, phase.

*This report reflects statements and concerns raised during the period of intensified conflict in Sri Lanka's Vanni region.*

**Sri Lanka Announces 48-Hour Humanitarian Pause as Civilian Toll Mounts, Press Access Criticized**

COLOMBO — The Sri Lankan government announced a 48-hour humanitarian pause in its military offensive against Tamil Tiger rebels on Monday, aimed at allowing civilians trapped in the shrinking conflict zone in the island's north to escape to safety, officials said.

The pause, set to begin at dawn, comes amid mounting international pressure over the fate of tens of thousands of Tamil civilians believed to be trapped alongside retreating Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) fighters in a narrow strip of coastal territory in the Vanni region. Aid agencies and the United Nations have repeatedly warned that civilians are caught in crossfire, with limited access to food, medicine, and clean water.

"We are calling on all civilians to use this window to move to safe zones designated by the government," a military spokesman said, though he did not specify how safe passage would be guaranteed or monitored.

Humanitarian organizations, while cautiously welcoming the pause, expressed skepticism that 48 hours would be sufficient to evacuate the estimated tens of thousands still trapped. The International Committee of the Red Cross and UN officials have previously accused both government forces and the LTTE of endangering civilian lives — the government through shelling of designated safe zones, and the rebels through allegations of using civilians as human shields to prevent their retreat.

The announcement comes as international criticism intensifies over Sri Lanka's severe restrictions on independent journalists and aid workers seeking access to the conflict zone. Human rights groups and press freedom organizations, including the Committee to Protect Journalists and Reporters Without Borders, have condemned the government's near-total blackout on independent reporting from the war zone, saying it has made it impossible to verify casualty figures or conditions on the ground.

"The lack of transparency is deeply troubling," said one Western diplomat in Colombo, speaking on condition of anonymity. "We are relying almost entirely on government statements, which makes independent verification of the humanitarian situation extremely difficult."

The government has defended the restrictions, citing security concerns and accusing foreign media of bias in favor of the rebels, who have waged a decades-long insurgency seeking an independent homeland for the island's Tamil minority.

The United Nations has estimated that thousands of civilians have been killed in recent months of fighting, though exact figures remain disputed. Colombo has dismissed casualty estimates from rights groups as exaggerated.

As the pause approaches, aid organizations say they remain on standby to deliver emergency supplies and facilitate evacuations, but caution that access will depend on cooperation from both the government and the LTTE — a prospect that remains uncertain given the collapse of previous ceasefire arrangements.

The conflict, one of Asia's longest-running civil wars, has drawn renewed global attention as government forces close in on the last remaining rebel-held territory, raising fears of a bloody final confrontation.

# UN and International Community React to Sri Lanka's Brief Ceasefire Amid Escalating Humanitarian Crisis

**COLOMBO** — The United Nations and international human rights organizations have called for a genuine, extended ceasefire in Sri Lanka following a brief pause in fighting between government forces and Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels, as concerns mount over the fate of tens of thousands of civilians trapped in the conflict zone.

## Background: A Quarter-Century of Civil War

Sri Lanka's civil war, which began in 1983, stands as one of Asia's longest-running conflicts. The LTTE, commonly known as the Tamil Tigers, has fought for an independent homeland for the country's Tamil minority in the north and east of the island, alleging decades of discrimination by the Sinhalese-majority government.

The conflict has claimed an estimated 70,000 to 100,000 lives over its course and displaced hundreds of thousands more. Previous ceasefire attempts, including a Norwegian-brokered truce signed in 2002, ultimately collapsed, with both sides trading accusations of violations. The government formally withdrew from that ceasefire agreement in January 2008, launching a renewed military offensive that has steadily reduced LTTE-held territory in the north.

## The Brief Ceasefire

The most recent pause in hostilities came as government forces closed in on remaining rebel-held areas, where an estimated 150,000 to 250,000 civilians remain trapped, according to UN estimates. The temporary halt was announced amid intense international pressure but reportedly lasted only a short period before fighting resumed, with both sides blaming each other for renewed violence.

UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and UN human rights chief Navi Pillay have repeatedly urged both the Sri Lankan government and the LTTE to allow safe passage for civilians and to permit humanitarian aid workers and independent media access to the conflict zone, which has been largely sealed off from outside observation.

## Human Shield Allegations

A central and highly disputed element of the crisis involves allegations that the LTTE has been preventing civilians from leaving the shrinking conflict zone, effectively using them as human shields against government attacks. Sri Lankan officials and some international observers have accused the Tigers of forcibly holding the civilian population to deter military strikes and maintain leverage in the conflict's final stages.

The LTTE has denied these accusations, instead blaming government forces for indiscriminate shelling of areas known to contain large civilian populations, including hospitals and designated "safe zones."

Independent verification of claims from both sides has proven extremely difficult, as journalists and humanitarian organizations have faced severe restrictions on access to the war zone. This information vacuum has fueled international concern that serious violations of international humanitarian law may be occurring largely unwitnessed.

## International Response

UN officials have stopped short of assigning definitive blame while pressing for:

- An extended humanitarian ceasefire to allow civilian evacuation
- Unimpeded access for aid organizations, including the ICRC and UN agencies
- Protection of civilians under international humanitarian law
- Independent monitoring of the conflict zone

Human rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International, have echoed these calls, warning of a potential humanitarian catastrophe and urging accountability for any violations committed by either party.

The Sri Lankan government has maintained that its military operations are aimed solely at defeating the LTTE and rescuing civilians held against their will, while asserting its right to pursue what it characterizes as a domestic counter-terrorism operation without foreign interference.

---

*This report reflects the situation as understood during this period of the conflict, which formally concluded in May 2009 with the military defeat of the LTTE. Post-war investigations, including a UN Panel of Experts report released in 2011, later examined allegations of serious violations of international law by both government and LTTE forces during the conflict's final phase.*

**UN Criticizes Sri Lanka's Brief Ceasefire as Insufficient Amid Growing Humanitarian Crisis**

*By [Staff Writer]*

COLOMBO, Sri Lanka — United Nations officials expressed sharp disappointment Thursday with Sri Lanka's decision to implement only a short-term truce in its conflict zone, warning that the limited ceasefire fails to address the escalating humanitarian catastrophe affecting more than 100,000 civilians trapped by ongoing fighting.

The government's brief pause in hostilities, announced earlier this week, was intended to allow civilians to flee the narrow strip of land in the country's north where fighting between government forces and rebel fighters has intensified in recent months. However, UN representatives say the window was far too short to provide meaningful relief.

"A 48-hour pause is simply inadequate given the scale of suffering we are witnessing," said a UN humanitarian spokesperson in Geneva. "Tens of thousands of people are trapped without adequate food, clean water, or medical care. A ceasefire measured in hours, not weeks, cannot resolve a crisis of this magnitude."

Aid organizations report that displaced civilians are sheltering in makeshift camps with severely limited access to basic necessities. Hospitals in the region have reportedly come under fire in recent weeks, further straining an already overwhelmed medical system. The UN has called for sustained humanitarian corridors to allow aid convoys safe passage and to enable civilians to evacuate without fear of violence.

Sri Lankan government officials have defended the shortened truce, citing security concerns and accusing rebel forces of using the ceasefire periods to regroup rather than allow civilian evacuations. Military spokespersons maintain that a prolonged halt in operations would jeopardize the safety of troops and undermine efforts to bring the decades-long conflict to a close.

Rights groups, however, argue that civilians are bearing the brunt of the continued fighting. The International Committee of the Red Cross has echoed the UN's concerns, noting that its own efforts to deliver aid and evacuate the wounded have been hampered by the fighting resuming so quickly after each truce period ends.

UN Secretary-General's office reiterated calls for both parties to agree to a more extended cessation of hostilities, emphasizing that the international community stands ready to assist with evacuations and the delivery of emergency supplies.

"The people trapped in this conflict zone did not choose this war," the UN statement read. "They deserve a genuine opportunity to reach safety, not a token gesture that leaves them exposed to continued danger."

As diplomatic pressure mounts, humanitarian agencies continue to warn that without a significant expansion of ceasefire terms, the death toll and suffering among displaced civilians will likely continue to rise in the coming weeks.

*This is a developing story.*
